title: Starship Flight Tracker
intro: Every SpaceX Starship integrated flight, from Flight 1 in April 2023 to the upcoming Flight 15, with goals, results, causes, lessons and costs. Times are Netherlands time (CET/CEST).
overview: 14 flights flown, the last one the first to reach orbit; the next is planned as the first catch of both stages.
timezoneNote: Times: local Netherlands time (CET = UTC+1 in winter, CEST = UTC+2 in summer). Starbase is on CDT (UTC-5) in summer and CST (UTC-6) in winter: CET = CST + 7 h.

next.timezone: Starbase is on CST (UTC−6); CET = CST + 7 h
next.plan: Orbit, then return both stages to Starbase for the first double tower catch
next.hardware: Both vehicles static-fired late October; ship rehearsed in the chopsticks in September
next.callout: Liftoff time is not announced yet and SpaceX has no Flight 15 mission page up. The time will be added here in CET once it is published.

laterCaption: Dates are no-earlier-than targets and will move.
laterNote: Musk has also said the flight after Flight 15 could refly the caught vehicles; NASASpaceflight expects Flight 16 to use B23 and S43 instead.
costNote: SpaceX has never published a per-flight cost. All figures here are estimates or programme totals, not a price for any single flight.
notes: Success and failure follow Wikipedia's launch-outcome column; SpaceX counts most flights as successful tests.
V1/V2/V3 follow SpaceX's generation names (Block 1/2/3). Flights 7–11 paired a V2 ship with a first-generation booster.
Times are converted from SpaceX's CT times or Wikipedia's UTC times to Europe/Amsterdam.
Flights 12–14 facts that only appear on Wikipedia or secondary sites are flagged inside each flight.

costMethod.text: Rough direct launch-resource estimates, NOT SpaceX figures, audited accounts, customer prices or statistical confidence intervals. USD, rounded planning ranges on a 2024–26 reference-cost basis; no inflation normalisation. Model = newly built flight hardware (engines already included) + refurbishment/replacement hardware on reflights + direct test/launch operations and propellant. Charge a new vehicle to its first flight, never again on reflight; no residual-value credit merely for catching it. This acquisition-at-first-use convention makes Flights 9/11 cheaper but is not depreciation or net hardware-loss accounting. Payload’s $90M full-stack/$63M booster/$27M ship benchmark, as reported by Motley Fool, is an extrapolative post-R&D production estimate, NOT measured prototype expenditure; BBC’s ~$100M/test-launch estimate is only a sanity check. Our component bounds and prototype allowances are explicit editorial assumptions, not quotes. Early V1: booster $55–85M + ship $30–45M + operations $5–20M = $90–150M. Other V1/V2 new stacks: $45–70M + $25–40M + $5–15M = $75–125M. Reused V1 booster/V2 ship: ship $25–40M + refurbishment/replacement engines $5–20M + operations $5–15M = $35–75M. V3 new: booster $40–80M + ship $25–45M + operations $5–15M = $70–140M; no claimed verified Raptor 3 saving. Future specialised transfer vehicle: ship $35–75M + booster $10–80M (reuse versus new) + operations $5–15M = $50–170M. HLS prototype/lander: ship $65–150M + booster $10–80M + operations $5–20M = $80–250M, an especially weak scenario allowance, not an independently measured HLS unit cost. All ranges exclude programme R&D, factory/pad construction, extraordinary ground damage/rebuild, payload manufacture (including Starlink), investigation/third-party compensation and non-Starship vehicles. HLS rows are ONE lander/prototype Earth launch each, NOT complete missions: depot and many tanker launches are extra. A future ordinary V3 flight with both vehicles genuinely reflown would instead be a $10–40M incremental scenario (refurbishment/replacements $5–25M + operations $5–15M), contingent on demonstrated reuse. All confidence low; future/HLS lower still. Midpoint is arithmetic, not a best forecast.
